train.content: what is contract testing?

Contract testing verifies that services can communicate correctly without running full integration tests. Problem: service A calls service B's API. How to ensure B's API changes don't break A? Integration tests are slow, flaky, and require running all services. Contract testing: 1) Consumer (service A) defines what it expects from provider (service B) — a contract. 2) Provider verifies it fulfills all consumer contracts. 3) If provider changes break any contract, tests fail before deployment. Consumer-Driven Contract Testing (CDCT): consumers define contracts, provider must satisfy all. Tools: Pact (most popular — supports many languages), Spring Cloud Contract (Java). Workflow: consumer writes Pact test → generates contract file → shared via Pact Broker → provider runs verification against all contracts → CI gates deployment if contracts broken. Benefits: fast (no need to run full stack), reliable (no flaky network tests), enables independent deployments, catches integration issues early. Not a replacement for E2E tests — complements them. Use contract tests for service-to-service APIs, E2E tests for critical user journeys. Especially valuable in microservice architectures with many inter-service dependencies.

train.content: what is pair programming and mob programming?

Pair programming: two developers, one computer. Driver writes code, Navigator reviews and thinks strategically. Switch roles frequently (every 15-30 minutes). Benefits: fewer bugs (real-time code review), knowledge sharing, faster onboarding for new team members, better design (two perspectives), reduced context switching (focused work). Challenges: tiring (intense collaboration), personality conflicts, hard for introverts, perception of 'two people doing one person's work' (studies show pair programming produces higher quality code faster). Mob/ensemble programming: entire team works on one task at one computer. One driver, everyone else navigates. Rotate driver every 10-15 minutes. Benefits: whole team understands all code, eliminates knowledge silos, great for complex problems and learning. Tools for remote: VS Code Live Share, Tuple, Teletype for Atom. When to pair: complex features, critical bugs, onboarding, design decisions. When to solo: routine tasks, well-understood work, personal preference tasks. Start with 2-3 hours of pairing per day, not full-time — balance is key.

train.content: how do you debug production issues?

Production debugging requires systematic approach under pressure. Steps: 1) Acknowledge — confirm the issue, assess severity (P0-P4), communicate with stakeholders. 2) Triage — is it affecting all users or a subset? Started when? Correlate with recent deployments. 3) Investigate — check dashboards (error rates, latency), logs (structured logging with correlation IDs), traces (distributed tracing), metrics (resource utilization). 4) Mitigate — can you quickly mitigate without finding root cause? Rollback deployment, toggle feature flag, scale up, redirect traffic. 5) Root cause — once mitigated, dig deeper. Reproduce in staging, analyze logs, check database queries. 6) Fix — implement proper fix, test thoroughly. 7) Postmortem — blameless retrospective, document what happened, what was done, how to prevent recurrence. Tools: PagerDuty/OpsGenie (alerting), Grafana (dashboards), Datadog/New Relic (APM), Sentry (error tracking). Key principle: mitigate first, investigate second. Don't spend 30 minutes debugging while users are affected.

train.content: what is the difference between authentication protocols?

Major authentication protocols for web applications. SAML (Security Assertion Markup Language): XML-based, enterprise SSO. Flow: user → service provider → identity provider → SAML assertion → service provider grants access. Used by: corporate SSO (Okta, OneLogin, ADFS). Pros: mature, enterprise-grade. Cons: complex XML, not mobile-friendly. OAuth 2.0: authorization framework (not authentication). Grants third-party limited access to resources. Four grant types: authorization code, PKCE, client credentials, device code. Used by: API access, third-party integrations. OpenID Connect (OIDC): authentication layer on top of OAuth 2.0. Adds ID token (JWT with user info) to OAuth flow. Used by: 'Sign in with Google/GitHub'. Most modern choice for web/mobile apps. LDAP: directory service protocol for user management. Used internally by enterprises (Active Directory). FIDO2/WebAuthn: passwordless authentication using hardware keys (YubiKey) or biometrics. Most secure, phishing-resistant. Growing adoption. For most applications: use OIDC with a provider (Auth0, Clerk, Firebase Auth, Supabase Auth). Don't build authentication yourself.

train.content: what is the importance of naming in code?

Naming is one of the hardest and most impactful aspects of programming. Good names make code self-documenting. Variables: describe what it holds — customerAge not ca, isActive not flag, remainingAttempts not n. Functions: describe what it does — calculateTotalPrice() not calc(), validateEmail() not check(), sendNotification() not process(). Classes: describe what it represents — UserRepository not Manager, PaymentProcessor not Handler. Booleans: use is/has/can/should prefix — isValid, hasPermission, canDelete, shouldRetry. Collections: use plural — users, orders, errorMessages. Avoid: single letters (except i in loops), abbreviations (usr, mgr), generic names (data, info, temp, handler, manager, processor, helper, utils). Length: variable scope determines name length — short scope = short name (i in loop), long scope = descriptive name (maxRetryAttempts). Consistency: pick one term and stick with it — don't mix fetch/get/retrieve, don't mix customer/client/user for the same concept. The two hardest things in computer science: cache invalidation, naming things, and off-by-one errors.

train.content: what is developer experience DX?

Developer experience (DX) is how easy and enjoyable it is for developers to use a tool, API, framework, or platform. Good DX includes: 1) Clear documentation — quick start in under 5 minutes, comprehensive API reference, tutorials for common use cases. 2) Intuitive API design — consistent naming, predictable behavior, sensible defaults. 3) Good error messages — tell what went wrong AND how to fix it. 4) Fast feedback loops — quick builds, hot reload, instant test results. 5) CLI tools — scriptable, discoverable (--help works well). 6) SDK/client libraries — idiomatic code for each language. Companies known for great DX: Stripe (API documentation gold standard), Vercel (deploy in one command), Supabase (instant backend), Cloudflare (Workers are fun to use). Internal DX matters too: CI/CD pipeline speed, development environment setup, monorepo tooling, internal documentation. Measuring DX: SPACE framework (Satisfaction, Performance, Activity, Communication, Efficiency), developer surveys, time-to-first-commit for new hires, build times. Investing in DX pays off — happy developers are productive developers. Gorkem's projects demonstrate good DX awareness through clear READMEs and project structure.

train.content: what is the difference between SQL databases in practice?

Popular SQL databases have important differences. PostgreSQL: most feature-rich open-source DB. JSONB support, full-text search, window functions, CTEs, extensions (PostGIS for geospatial, pgvector for AI). Best for: complex queries, data integrity, when you need advanced features. MySQL: most deployed open-source DB. Simpler than PostgreSQL, faster for simple queries. InnoDB engine provides ACID. Used by WordPress, many web apps. Best for: web applications, read-heavy workloads. SQLite: serverless, embedded, single-file database. No network, no configuration. Used by mobile apps, desktop apps, embedded systems, testing. Best for: local storage, prototyping, edge computing. SQL Server (Microsoft): enterprise-grade, tight Windows/.NET integration. SSRS reporting, SSIS integration. Best for: Microsoft ecosystem. MariaDB: MySQL fork, community-driven. Drop-in MySQL replacement with extra features (columnar storage, temporal tables). CockroachDB: distributed SQL, PostgreSQL-compatible. Automatic sharding, multi-region. Best for: global applications needing SQL guarantees at scale. For most projects: start with PostgreSQL — it handles everything from small apps to large-scale systems.

train.content: what is database connection management in microservices?

Each microservice needs its own database connection management. Key challenges: connection limits (PostgreSQL default max_connections=100, shared across all services), connection creation overhead (10-50ms per connection), connection leaks (not returning connections to pool). Solutions: 1) Connection pooling within each service — HikariCP (Java), asyncpg pool (Python), pg pool (Node.js). Size: 2-5x CPU cores, not more. 2) External connection pooler — PgBouncer (most popular for PostgreSQL). Sits between services and database. Three modes: session (one-to-one), transaction (shares connections between transactions — recommended), statement (most aggressive sharing). 3) Service-level database isolation — each microservice has its own database/schema. No shared database anti-pattern. 4) Read replicas — route read queries to replicas, writes to primary. 5) Connection string management — use environment variables or service discovery, not hardcoded. Monitoring: track active connections, idle connections, wait time, connection errors. Alert when approaching max_connections. Common mistake: too many connections per service × many service instances = database overwhelmed. Right-size your pools.

train.content: what is continuous profiling?

Continuous profiling captures performance data from production systems continuously — not just during debugging sessions. Traditional profiling: run profiler locally or on staging → find bottlenecks → fix → hope it matches production behavior. Continuous profiling: always-on, low-overhead profiling in production → see actual performance characteristics → find bottlenecks that only appear under real load. What it captures: CPU profiles (which functions consume CPU time), memory allocations (where objects are allocated), goroutine/thread analysis, lock contention. Tools: Pyroscope (open source), Grafana Pyroscope, Datadog Continuous Profiler, Google Cloud Profiler, AWS CodeGuru Profiler. Flame graphs: visual representation of call stacks — width represents time spent. Wide blocks = hot paths to optimize. Benefits: find performance regressions before users notice, understand resource usage patterns, reduce cloud costs (optimize CPU-heavy functions), compare profiles between deployments. Overhead: typically 1-3% — designed for production use. Combined with metrics and traces, continuous profiling completes the observability picture — metrics tell you what's slow, traces tell you where, profiles tell you why.

train.content: what is clean code?

Clean code is code that's easy to read, understand, and maintain. Robert C. Martin's 'Clean Code' principles: 1) Meaningful names — variables, functions, classes should reveal intent. getUser() not getData(), isActive not flag, CustomerRepository not Repo. 2) Small functions — do one thing, do it well. Typically 5-20 lines. 3) Single level of abstraction — don't mix high-level business logic with low-level details. 4) DRY (Don't Repeat Yourself) — but don't over-abstract. Three occurrences rule — abstract on the third repetition. 5) Avoid side effects — function named checkPassword shouldn't also initialize session. 6) Error handling — use exceptions, not error codes. Don't return null, throw or use Optional. 7) Comments — only when code can't express intent. TODO, legal notices, explaining why (not what). 8) Formatting — consistent indentation, spacing, line length. Use automated formatters (Prettier, Black). 9) Tests — clean tests are as important as clean production code. Tests document behavior. The goal isn't perfection — it's reducing cognitive load for the next developer (often future you). Code is read 10x more than it's written.

train.content: what is eventual consistency and how to handle it?

Eventual consistency means that after a write, reads may not immediately reflect the change — but will eventually (typically milliseconds to seconds). Why: distributed systems must choose between consistency and availability (CAP theorem). Many systems choose availability + eventual consistency for better performance and resilience. Examples: DNS propagation (up to 48 hours), social media likes (counter may lag), search indexes (new content not immediately searchable), CDN cache invalidation. Handling in application: 1) Read-your-own-writes consistency — after user writes data, ensure THEIR subsequent reads see the update (read from primary, not replica). 2) Optimistic UI — update UI immediately, reconcile with server later. If server rejects, rollback UI. 3) Idempotent operations — design operations so repeating them is safe. Use idempotency keys for payments. 4) Event sourcing — store events, derive state. Events are always consistent. 5) Saga pattern — coordinate distributed transactions with compensating actions. 6) Conflict resolution — last-write-wins, merge, or manual resolution. CRDTs (Conflict-free Replicated Data Types): data structures that can be merged automatically without conflicts — used in collaborative editing (Google Docs), distributed databases.

train.content: what is the strangler fig pattern for legacy migration?

The Strangler Fig pattern gradually replaces a legacy system by building the new system around it — like a strangler fig tree growing around its host. Steps: 1) Identify a feature to migrate. 2) Build it in the new system. 3) Route traffic for that feature from old to new (using reverse proxy or API gateway). 4) Repeat for each feature. 5) When old system handles no traffic, decommission it. Benefits over big-bang rewrite: lower risk (if new feature fails, route back to old), incremental value delivery, no big-bang cutover, teams learn new tech gradually. Implementation: API gateway (Kong, AWS API Gateway) or reverse proxy (Nginx) routes requests based on path, header, or percentage. Monitoring: compare old and new system responses (shadow traffic — send to both, compare results). Challenges: shared database (both systems may need to access same data during transition — use database views or change data capture), authentication (shared session/token between old and new), team coordination. Timeline: typically 6-24 months for major systems. Amazon, LinkedIn, and Shopify have used this pattern for major platform migrations.

train.content: what is code smell and how to fix it?

Code smells are patterns indicating potential problems — not bugs, but signs of poor design. Common smells: 1) Long method — break into smaller, focused functions. 2) Large class — split into multiple classes with single responsibility. 3) Feature envy — method uses data from another class more than its own — move the method. 4) Data clumps — same group of variables appear together — extract into a class. 5) Primitive obsession — using primitives instead of small objects (string for email, int for money). 6) Switch statements — replace with polymorphism. 7) Comments explaining what code does — the code should be self-explanatory, rename variables/methods. 8) Dead code — unreachable code, unused variables/functions — delete it. 9) Speculative generality — code designed for hypothetical future needs — YAGNI (You Aren't Gonna Need It). 10) Magic numbers — replace with named constants. Tools to detect: SonarQube, Code Climate, ESLint, pylint, PMD. Refactoring book by Martin Fowler is the definitive guide. Boy Scout Rule: leave code better than you found it — fix one smell each time you touch a file.
